meta.title: Girgaoncha Raja
meta.institution: Nikadwari Lane Sarvajanik Shree Ganeshotsav Mandal
meta.location: Nikadwari Lane, Girgaon, Mumbai 400004; office: 9 Khedekar Sadan, opposite Jain Hospital
meta.foundedNote: Official institutional history dates the mandal to 1928.
meta.intro: Girgaoncha Raja belongs to the Nikadwari Lane mandal established in 1928, a separate institution from Keshavji Naik Chawl. Its archive centres on large Shadu-clay idols, a recognisable Maharashtrian pheta and a multigenerational sculpting tradition. Contemporary reports connect bamboo, grass and basketry to the making process. This foundation records those material choices and dated idol views while treating height records and environmental claims as year-specific statements by their named sources.

paragraphs.text: The mandal's 1928 foundation belongs to Nikadwari Lane, not to the 1893 Keshavji Naik Chawl celebration. Its official retrospective links the organisation to Tilak's public-festival ideals and records continuing social, educational and cultural work. Spelling variants such as Nikatdwari and Girgaum must be searchable without merging separate institutions.

The environmental reputation has a traceable public milestone: the Prime Minister's 28 August 2016 Mann Ki Baat transcript names Girgaoncha Raja among groups promoting clay idols. The primary transcript takes precedence over a later report's 2017 date. This is evidence of recognition, not an independent lifecycle assessment of every year's celebration.

The 2024 making account describes clay, bamboo, grass and handwoven baskets, with a turbaned seated idol reported at 21 feet. Contemporary Marathi coverage in 2025 again names Shadu clay, grass and baskets. These details make the armature, material procurement and immersion apparatus as important to preserve as the finished front view.

A 2019 report associates the idol with Patkar-family craftsmanship and a large Kolhapuri-style pheta. The 2026 gallery names Rajan Vishnupant Patkar within a four-generation lineage and shows a seated yellow-dhoti form with an elaborate blue-and-gold turban. Changing reported heights should remain attached to their years and measurement conventions.

sections.title: Following the pheta and its makers across recorded years

paragraphs.text: The 2012 Rediff report connects its pictured clay idol to Nikadvari Lane and names Rajan Patkar as that year's sculptor. This gives a dated maker attribution without assigning one individual to every historical idol. A later Rediff page republishes the same photograph; its publication in 2013 does not create a second captured year.

Mumbai Live's 2019 retrospective supplies four expressly year-labelled views: 2015, 2016, 2018 and 2019. The photographed street and pandal settings provide evidence of physical scenes, while the dates remain the publisher's attributions. The 2014 blog contributes a printed invitation and a feet-worship ceremony scene, which are distinct from a complete installation portrait.

A Marathi Pudhari report describes the 2025 pheta's fabric construction and its 27 August unveiling. The claimed recognition belongs to the named World Records Book of India; the archive does not independently certify a worldwide superlative. Bridgestone's own September 2025 campaign statement identifies Rajan Patkar in its Girgaoncha Raja craft film, adding a primary contemporary maker link.

claims.text: This is the Nikadwari Lane institution founded in 1928.
The primary Mann Ki Baat recognition date is 28 August 2016.
Clay, bamboo, grass and baskets are documented making materials.
The 2024 height and record certification are year-specific reported claims.
The 2026 source names the Patkar lineage and current sculptor.
The 2012 report specifically names Rajan Patkar for that year's Girgaoncha Raja idol.
The 2025 corporate film-maker statement identifies Rajan Patkar with Girgaoncha Raja.
claims.status: primary campaign statement; limited to its subject

researchNotes.coverage: Institutional record, primary 2016 government transcript, Marathi materials reporting and two inspected dated press images. Phase 2: 7 annual entries supplemented after direct image inspection; source labels and photographic appearance assessed separately.
gaps: No continuous annual photographic sequence; most years before 2012 and pandemic-year installations remain unfilled.
2015/2016/2018/2019 years are explicit retrospective publisher labels, not authenticated camera dates.
2014 materials document a ceremony and an invitation; the invitation's incorporated idol picture has no established capture year.

Indian Express 2022 and 2023 Girgaon-captioned candidates are withheld: their depicted forms differ from corroborated examples and exact institution/year identity needs further checking. A changing form alone does not prove the captions false.
Original sculptor contracts, festival souvenirs and individual photo credits are still needed; 2025 record-book recognition has not been independently certified.
Unknown reuse rights for photographs and designed objects.
nextActions: Confirm sculptor-family chronology and individual photo credits.
Preserve dated making and immersion sequences, not just first-look portraits.
